position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed consumer vs emergency preparedness messaging test (X1) to gather evidence on purchase intent before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) targeting individual buyers.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line without a new consumer proposition (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partner with outdoor retailers, target emergency preparedness organizations) while retaining the core technology.
4) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing markets.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote activities, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that signals distress to search and rescue.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) who need reliable emergency communication in remote areas.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of remote-area risks and a willingness to invest in safety equipment that can save lives.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell premium-priced consumer beacons directly to individuals, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in 2002 were sufficient to create a market for distress beacons.
Consumers associate 406 MHz beacons with emergency capability and are willing to pay more for that capability.
Distribution channels (e.g., outdoor retailers) can reach this segment effectively.
predictions: If offered a consumer beacon priced at $300-$500, at least 10% of surveyed outdoor recreationists would express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Sales of a consumer beacon would be positively correlated with outdoor recreation participation rates in a given region.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote activities, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that signals distress to search and rescue.

T2.claim: Emergency preparedness organizations (e.g., search and rescue teams, disaster response agencies) will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they need reliable, interoperable communication for remote operations, and they are willing to invest in technology that enhances operational safety.
T2.who_benefits: Emergency preparedness organizations (national SAR teams, FEMA, local emergency management offices) that require reliable distress communication in remote or hazardous environments.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing recognition of the need for standardized, satellite-based distress communication to improve response efficiency and reduce casualty rates.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell bulk contracts or subscription-based services to these organizations, capturing volume sales and recurring revenue.
assumptions: Emergency preparedness budgets in 2002 allocated funds for new communication equipment.
Interoperability between different emergency services is a critical purchase criterion.
Distress beacons are viewed as a safety-critical component rather than a consumer toy.
predictions: If offered a bulk contract for 50 beacons at $1,200 each, at least 15% of surveyed emergency preparedness organizations would place an order within 12 weeks.
Purchase decisions would be influenced by the ability of beacons to work with existing SAR radio systems.
T2.first_claim: Emergency preparedness organizations (e.g., search and rescue teams, disaster response agencies) will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they need reliable, interoperable communication for remote operations, and they are willing to invest in technology that enhances operational safety.

assessments.quote: The 406 MHz PLB is primarily intended to provide a distress and alerting capacity for use by the general public in life threatening situations in a remote environment after all other means of notifying SAR responders (e.g., telephone, radio) have been exhausted.
assessments.does_not_show: It does not show that outdoor recreationists specifically adopt distress beacons or that they are willing to pay a premium for them.

X1.name: Consumer vs Emergency Preparedness Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 outdoor recreationists (recruited via outdoor activity forums) and 250 emergency preparedness organization personnel (recruited via SAR agency and FEMA contacts)
X1.measure: Purchase intent: percentage of respondents who would buy the simulated product within 12 weeks

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor recreationists exposed to consumer messaging will show purchase intent >=10% (150/250). Emergency preparedness respondents will show purchase intent <5%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Emergency preparedness respondents exposed to emergency messaging will show purchase intent >=15% (37/250). Outdoor recreationists will show purchase intent <10%.

X1.decision_rule: If outdoor recreation purchase intent >=10% AND emergency purchase intent <5%, proceed with consumer proposition. If emergency purchase intent >=15% AND outdoor purchase intent <10%, proceed with emergency proposition. If both >=10% or both <5%,

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, purchase intent, or willingness to pay for distress beacons. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed consumer vs emergency preparedness messaging test (X1) to gather evidence on purchase intent before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) who need reliable emergency communication in remote areas
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced 406 MHz distress beacon that signals distress to search and rescue, marketed as a safety necessity for remote activities.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week online survey with 500 respondents (250 outdoor recreationists, 250 emergency preparedness personnel) to measure purchase intent under consumer and emergency messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay, and the potential for emergency preparedness organizations to adopt beacons.
would_change_if: If the test shows outdoor purchase intent >=10% and emergency purchase intent <5%, proceed with consumer proposition.
If the test shows emergency purchase intent >=15% and outdoor purchase intent <10%, proceed with emergency proposition.
If both groups show purchase intent >=10%, reconsider a dual‑market approach.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed consumer vs government purchase intent test (X1) to validate demand before committing resources. If the test shows outdoor recreationists meet both WTP and purchase intent thresholds, proceed to develop a consumer product; otherwise, focus on B2B/B2G markets or other routes to market.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case leveraging its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) targeting individual buyers.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line without a new consumer proposition (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group (e.g., partner with outdoor retailers, target emergency preparedness organizations) while retaining the core technology.
4) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing markets.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote activities, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that signals distress to search and rescue.
T1.who_benefits: Individual outdoor recreationists (hikers, climbers, kayakers) who need reliable emergency communication in remote areas.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing awareness of remote-area risks and a willingness to invest in safety equipment that can save lives.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell premium-priced consumer beacons directly to individuals, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in 2002 were sufficient to create a market for distress beacons.
Consumers associate 406 MHz beacons with safety and reliability.
Price sensitivity is low for a life-saving device.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreationists will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price above $300.
Sales of ACR’s consumer beacon will be concentrated among users who frequently travel in remote locations.
Willingness to pay will be positively correlated with perceived risk of remote travel.
T1.first_claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they view them as a safety necessity for remote activities, and they are willing to pay a premium for a product that signals distress to search and rescue.

T2.claim: Emergency preparedness organizations (e.g., search and rescue teams, disaster response agencies) will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they need reliable, interoperable communication for remote operations, and they are willing to invest in technology that improves mission success.
T2.who_benefits: Emergency preparedness organizations (national SAR teams, FEMA, local emergency management offices) that require reliable distress communication in remote or hazardous environments.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing recognition of the need for standardized, satellite-based distress communication to reduce response time and improve safety in remote areas.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell bulk or subscription-based beacons to government agencies and NGOs, capturing volume sales and recurring revenue from maintenance contracts.
assumptions: Government procurement cycles for emergency equipment were active in 2002.
Interoperability standards for distress beacons existed or were emerging.
Budget for emergency preparedness equipment was allocated to life-saving technology.
predictions: Government procurement requests for 406 MHz distress beacons will increase in 2002.
Sales to emergency preparedness organizations will be concentrated in regions with high SAR activity or disaster-prone areas.
Willingness to pay will be influenced by the need for interoperability and reliability in remote operations.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a time‑saving message (e.g., "Reduce yard work time by 50% with a lawn tractor") or a status message (e.g., "Join the elite 10% of homeowners with a John Deere lawn tractor, a sign of affluence and social standing"). Participants are asked about purchase intent ("Would you buy this tractor?" on a 1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (maximum price).
X1.sample: 200 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region. Randomly assigned to either time‑saving or status message condition (100 per condition).

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and current reach to individual buyers (unknown from dossier).
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home‑garden, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering tractors directly to individual buyers through dealers.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on farm, combine, and industrial equipment sales through dealers.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., mobile equipment manufacturers).

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a convenient, time‑saving tool for yard work, and they are willing to purchase directly from Deere if the price is competitive with other brands.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking efficient yard care; Deere gains sales and brand recognition in the consumer market.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing suburban population and increasing disposable income make yard work a visible, time‑critical task; a tractor offers faster mowing than hand tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors directly to consumers through dealers, capturing margin on each unit and building brand loyalty that can be leveraged for future sales.
assumptions: Suburban growth in the 1960s increases demand for yard care.
Homeowners perceive lawn tractors as a status symbol and are willing to pay a premium.
Deere can produce tractors at a cost that allows a competitive price point.
predictions: If Deere launches a consumer‑focused lawn tractor with a price comparable to leading consumer brands, sales will exceed 5,000 units in the first year.
Consumer surveys will show that at least 30% of homeowners who currently use hand tools would switch to a tractor if price were similar.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a convenient, time‑saving tool for yard work, and they are willing to purchase directly from Deere if the price is competitive with other brands.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a status symbol and a symbol of modern, comfortable living, and they are willing to purchase them even if the price is higher than functional alternatives.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking to signal wealth and modern lifestyle; Deere gains premium sales and brand prestige.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Post‑World War II suburban growth creates a culture of consumerism and aspirational products; a tractor is seen as a visible marker of success and modernity.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells tractors at premium prices through dealers, capturing higher margins and building a luxury brand that can be leveraged for future premium offerings.
assumptions: Suburban homeowners associate lawn care with modern, comfortable living.
Price sensitivity is lower for status‑driven buyers.
Deere can position tractors as a lifestyle product rather than purely functional.
predictions: If Deere launches a consumer‑focused lawn tractor priced 20% above leading consumer brands, early adopters will purchase at a rate of at least 1,000 units in the first year.
Surveyed homeowners will rank "status" as the top reason for considering a tractor purchase, even when functional alternatives are cheaper.

X1.name: Retail vs. Dealer Distribution Test
X1.method: Randomly assign 200 homeowners in a mid‑size city to one of two groups. Group A receives a Deere lawn tractor through a retail hardware store (offered as a bundle with a garden tool). Group B receives the same tractor through a Deere dealer. Both groups are offered a limited‑time discount of 10% and a warranty. Track whether each group purchases the tractor within 12 weeks.
X1.sample: 200 homeowners (100 per group) recruited via local hardware stores and community centers.
X1.measure: Purchase conversion rate (percentage of participants who buy the tractor) within 12 weeks.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A (retail) will have a higher conversion rate than Group B (dealer) because homeowners view the tractor as a convenient, multipurpose tool and are willing to buy it through retail channels.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B (dealer) will have a higher conversion rate than Group A (retail) because homeowners receive the tractor as a gift or incentive from a trusted retailer, reducing perceived cost and increasing social pressure.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s conversion rate is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B’s, T1 is supported. If Group B’s conversion rate is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group A’s, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 15 points, both theories remain uncertain.

arguments.name: Retail vs. Dealer Distribution Test
arguments.method: Randomly assign 200 homeowners in a mid‑size city to one of two groups. Group A receives a Deere lawn tractor through a retail hardware store (offered as a bundle with a garden tool). Group B receives the same tractor through a Deere dealer. Both groups are offered a limited‑time discount of 10% and a warranty. Track whether each group purchases the tractor within 12 weeks.
arguments.sample: 200 homeowners (100 per group) recruited via local hardware stores and community centers.
arguments.measure: Purchase conversion rate (percentage of participants who buy the tractor) within 12 weeks.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A (retail) will have a higher conversion rate than Group B (dealer) because homeowners view the tractor as a convenient, multipurpose tool and are willing to buy it through retail channels.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B (dealer) will have a higher conversion rate than Group A (retail) because homeowners receive the tractor as a gift or incentive from a trusted retailer, reducing perceived cost and increasing social pressure.

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A’s conversion rate is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B’s, T1 is supported. If Group B’s conversion rate is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group A’s, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 15 points, both theories remain uncertain.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Retail vs. Dealer Distribution Test (or a smaller pilot) to measure purchase conversion rates before committing resources. If the test shows retail distribution yields a 15%+ higher conversion than dealer distribution, proceed to develop a consumer proposition; otherwise, maintain focus on farm and industrial markets.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and current reach to individual buyers (unknown from dossier).
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home‑garden, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering tractors directly to individual buyers through dealers.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on existing farm, combine, and industrial equipment markets.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., mobile equipment manufacturers).

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors if they perceive them as a convenient, multipurpose tool that reduces labor costs and increases property value.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking to maintain yards and gardens efficiently.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If homeowners view the tractor as a time-saving, versatile asset rather than a specialized farm machine, they will purchase it to handle multiple tasks (e.g., mowing, tilling, snow removal).
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can capture value by selling tractors at premium prices, offering accessories, and building a brand associated with home‑yard efficiency.
assumptions: Homeowners have sufficient disposable income to afford a tractor.
They are aware of Deere's presence in the consumer market.
They trust Deere's engineering for non‑farm tasks.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay a price premium for a tractor marketed as a home‑yard tool.
Purchase intent will be higher when the tractor is presented as a multipurpose solution rather than a farm machine.
Sales of accessories (e.g., mower decks, tillers) will be higher when sold with the tractor.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors if they perceive them as a convenient, multipurpose tool that reduces labor costs and increases property value.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they are introduced by established dealer networks that already serve their farm and industrial needs, reducing the perceived risk of purchasing a new product.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: If dealers offer a tractor as part of their existing product mix, homeowners trust the brand and are willing to purchase it because they already know the dealer and trust its expertise in equipment.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can capture value by leveraging its existing dealer network to sell tractors, potentially at higher margins due to the dealer's role in training and service, and by bundling accessories through the same channel.

X1.name: Dealer-Based vs. Independent Purchase Test
X1.method: Randomly assign 200 homeowners in a mid-size city (e.g., 50,000 residents) to two groups. Group A receives a brochure describing a new lawn and garden tractor as a multipurpose home‑yard tool, emphasizing time‑saving and versatility. Group B receives the same brochure but also receives a personal visit from a John Deere dealer who offers to sell the tractor and provides a 10% discount. Both groups have 12 weeks to decide whether to purchase the tractor. Track actual purchase decisions and willingness to pay.
X1.sample: 200 homeowners (100 per group) recruited via local newspapers and community boards.
X1.measure: Purchase decision (yes/no) and willingness to pay (price range offered).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show a higher purchase rate than Group B because the brochure message emphasizes convenience and multipurpose use.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show a higher purchase rate than Group A because the dealer visit and discount create a trusted, convenient purchase channel.

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase rate is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B’s, T1 is supported. If Group B’s purchase rate is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group A’s, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 15 points, both theories remain uncertain.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address homeowner purchase drivers or dealer involvement. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and current reach to individual buyers (unknown from dossier).
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home‑garden, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering tractors directly to individual buyers through dealers.
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on farm, combine, and industrial equipment sales through dealers.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., mobile equipment manufacturers).

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Utility vs Status Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a lawn tractor product description: one emphasizing "utility" (time‑saving, efficient yard work) and one emphasizing "status" (modern lifestyle, symbol of affluence). Each version includes a price point (e.g., $1,500) and a brief description of the tractor’s features. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the tractor and, if so, the likelihood of doing so (1‑10 scale).
X1.sample: 200 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region. Randomly assigned to view either the utility version or the status version.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each version. Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) difference between versions.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Utility version will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than the status version, because homeowners prioritize time‑saving and price sensitivity.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status version will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than the utility version, because homeowners seek a modern lifestyle symbol and are willing to pay a premium for status.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer motivations, price sensitivity, or demand for lawn tractors. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent for utility vs status messaging before committing resources. If the test shows a ≥1.5-point difference in purchase intent, develop a differentiated utility-focused proposition; otherwise, maintain the existing dealer-based model.
final.target_customer: Homeowners seeking efficient yard care (utility segment) or status-driven buyers (status segment).
final.value_proposition: A lawn tractor positioned as a time‑saving utility tool (for the utility segment) or as a modern lifestyle symbol (for the status segment), sold through existing dealer network with premium pricing if demand justifies it.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the €15,000 budget and 12‑week timeline.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer motivations and price sensitivity in 1962.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥1.5‑point difference in purchase intent favoring the status version, shift focus to a status‑driven proposition.
If the test shows no significant difference, maintain the existing dealer model without differentiation.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Utility vs Status Messaging
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a lawn tractor product description: one emphasizing "utility" (time‑saving, efficient yard work) and one emphasizing "status" (modern lifestyle, symbol of affluence). Each version includes a price point (e.g., $1,500) and a brief description of the tractor’s features. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the tractor and, if so, the likelihood of doing so (1‑10 scale).
arguments.sample: 200 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region. Randomly assigned to view either the utility version or the status version.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each version. Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) difference between versions.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Utility version will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than the status version, because homeowners prioritize time‑saving and price sensitivity.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Status version will generate higher purchase intent and WTP than the utility version, because homeowners seek a modern lifestyle symbol and are willing to pay a premium for status.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between the two versions exceeds 1.5 points on the 10‑point scale, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting the higher‑intent segment. If the difference is less than 1.5 points,

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent for utility vs status messaging before committing resources. If the test shows a ≥1.5-point difference in purchase intent, develop a differentiated utility-focused proposition; otherwise, maintain the existing dealer-based model.
